references.text: The same wording appears earlier in the parable: the prodigal son 'was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found' ([ref:Luk 15:24|Luke 15:24]). Verse 32 repeats this as a reason given to the older brother.
In the parable of the lost sheep, there is an invitation to rejoice when what was lost is found ([ref:Luk 15:6-7|Luke 15:6-7]). The entire chapter 15 has joy over the recovered as a recurring theme.
In the parable of the lost coin, there is an invitation to rejoice when what was lost is found ([ref:Luk 15:9-10|Luke 15:9-10]), and it is linked to the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

God does not delight in the death of the wicked, but that they turn from their ways and live ([ref:Esek 18:23|Ezekiel 18:23]). The father's joy in the parable reflects God's desire for repentance rather than judgment.

'As surely as I live,' declares the Sovereign Lord, 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live' ([ref:Esek 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11]). God's joy over repentance is the background for the father's call to celebrate.

Paul describes how believers were 'dead' in their trespasses and sins, but God has made them alive with Christ ([ref:Ef 2:1-5|Ephesians 2:1-5]). The image of moving from death to life corresponds with the words about the prodigal son.
Believers are urged to present themselves to God 'as those who have been brought from death to life' ([ref:Rom 6:13|Romans 6:13]). The transition from death to life is used as a picture of salvation.

'We know that we have passed from death to life' ([ref:1 Joh 3:14|1 John 3:14]). The transition from spiritual death to life is a central New Testament theme that echoes in the parable's language about 'dead and alive'.

The context for the whole parable: tax collectors and sinners came near to Jesus, while the Pharisees and teachers of the law muttered ([ref:Luk 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2]). The older brother's attitude reflects the Pharisees' resistance to Jesus welcoming sinners.

Jesus says 'Let the dead bury their own dead' ([ref:Luk 9:60|Luke 9:60]), where 'dead' is used in a figurative, spiritual sense—the same linguistic image found in 'this brother of yours was dead and has come to life'.
